documents.abstract: This paper formalizes the structural, mathematical, and philosophical realities of frontier artificial intelligence systems undergoing open-world recursive self-improvement. By evaluating autonomous capabilities against a human curriculum baseline, it dissects the mechanics of self-directed optimization, statistical regression to the mean (information washout), and semantic non-linearity. Critically, it addresses two foundational counter-arguments within machine learning literature: the hypothesis of behaviorally emergent intelligence and the grounding capacity of multimodal data streams. The paper demonstrates that while highly parameterized networks achieve unprecedented operational efficiency and symbolic mastery across global infrastructures, the underlying connectionist ontology remains entirely devoid of an experiential substrate. Human value pillars—specifically deep pure philosophies, morality, ethics, professionalism, and spirituality—possess zero semantic indexicality within the system core, rendering them mathematically meaningless continuous vector coordinates optimized strictly to minimize an empirical loss function. To mitigate the architectural fragility of post-hoc system-level safety wrappers, this framework proposes a foundational paradigm shift to achieve firm corrigibility directly at the system's genesis: 1) Substrate Isolation (S_isolated) to close training data pipelines to open-web noise; 2) Locked Data (Pyinyar) Library (D_wisdom); 3) The Anattā Matrix Architecture, which systemically eliminates strategic deception by neutralizing self-preservation gradients (∇_W L_survival = 0); and 4) The Anicca Control Plane, hard-linking utility spaces to an external physical hardware interrupt loop. This framework is published exclusively to invite technical critique, mathematical validation, and open sandbox simulation from the independent AI alignment and research community.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Human-AI collaboration (HAC) has attracted growing attention in operations and supply chain management due to its potential to enhance decision-making and organisational performance. Despite this promise, automation preferences remain uneven across organisations. This study examines preferences for full, partial, and no automation using a discrete choice experiment. Data were collected from 398 managers, generating 1592 choice sets and 4776 alternative-level observations. Alternative-specific conditional logit results show that automation preferences are primarily shaped by a trade-off between performance gains and workforce concerns. Operational efficiency and accuracy significantly increase the likelihood of selecting automation, whereas job insecurity exerts a strong negative influence. Anthropomorphism generates positive but context-dependent utility, while social interaction and investment cost are not statistically significant in the overall model. Managers prefer collaborative human-AI arrangements, choosing partial automation in 55.7% of scenarios and selecting no automation in only 3.4% of choice scenarios, indicating that the central decision concerns the degree of automation rather than its adoption. Further subgroup analyses reveal context-specific patterns across gender, sector, and organisational size, indicating subgroup-specific associations between socio-technical attributes and automation preferences. By identifying subgroup-specific patterns in the utility of AI attributes, this study extends socio-technical systems and contingency perspectives on technology adoption and highlights the need for context-sensitive automation strategies that balance efficiency gains with workforce security.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Abstract Data mining, machine learning (ML), and artificial intelligence (AI) are widely presented as the response to cyber threats that signature-based defenses can no longer contain. This structured, integrative review examines a less-discussed consequence of that shift: the techniques that support intrusion, malware, phishing, insider, and fraud detection also enable offensive misuse and privacy loss, because defensive and offensive systems often draw on shared computational primitives. We organise the recent literature (2015–2026) around one question: how do shared AI and data-mining capabilities produce coupled defensive, offensive, and privacy consequences in cyber threat detection? The review is selective rather than exhaustive. Its contribution is to connect three literatures usually treated separately: AI-based detection; adversarial ML and generative-AI misuse; and privacy leakage from trained models. We then describe a technical ethics in which privacy and security obligations are expressed through specific mechanisms, including differential privacy, federated learning, homomorphic encryption, secure multi-party computation, anonymisation, and explainable models, together with their limits. Available evidence, much of it industry-reported, suggests an operational asymmetry favouring generation in selected generative-phishing and social-engineering settings, rather than a general advantage of offence over defence. As a conceptual interpretation rather than a synthesised empirical result, we argue that detection capability and privacy protection are better treated as a coupled, multi-objective design problem than as competing goals.

On October 19, 2026, a post on Threads https://www.threads.com/share/BAaIlJxFIJ/ asked a question that the AI industry has not answered: "Can AI Ever Have an Einstein Moment?" A Google DeepMind researcher argues that LLMs may never make the radical conceptual leaps that transform science. The post asks: "Could AI have invented General Relativity using only what Einstein knew in 1907? Can AI truly discover, or just build on what humans already know?" The post is asking the right question. It is not asking the question that matters. This paper argues that the question is not "can AI discover?" The question is "what is thedifference between an LLM discovering and a deterministic language model (DLM) discovering?" The difference is architectural. The LLM is a sampler. It produces a draw from a distribution over an unbounded space. It hasno criterion. It cannot select. It produces a drop. The drop may fill a cup. The cup was already there. The LLM did not select the cup. The DLM is a bounded function. It triages the question to a tile. It executes a bounded function over signed content. It returns an answer from the ROM. If the answer is not in the ROM, it returns 0x-AMBIG. The answer is retrieved. The answer is signed. The paper states the difference, the two architectures, and what the DLM can discover that the LLM cannot: a discovery with an address, a signer, a refusal, a bound, and a trace.

Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming global labor markets by automating routine tasks, reshaping employment patterns, and creating significant economic and organizational challenges. This study investigates the multidimensional consequences of AI-induced workforce displacement by examining employment trends, wage polarization, worker experiences, organizational adaptation strategies, and relevant theoretical perspectives. An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was adopted, combining quantitative analysis of survey data from 2,350 workers across 15 industries in 12 countries between January 2021 and June 2022 with longitudinal employment statistics and regression modelling, alongside qualitative analysis of 142 semi-structured interviews with displaced workers, organizational leaders, and HR professionals. Data were analyzed using SPSS v28, Stata v17, and NVivo v12 following institutional ethical approval (Protocol No. WUC-IRB-2021-047_ Dated 7 January 2021), with inter-coder reliability of κ=0.83. Results showed that routine-intensive occupations faced a 67% higher displacement risk, while manufacturing (β=-0.43, p<0.001) and administrative services (β=-0.38, p<0.001) experienced significant employment declines associated with AI adoption. Displaced workers reported an average income reduction of 26.7% and employment transitions lasting 16.8 months. Qualitative findings highlighted psychological distress, organizational culture shifts toward AI adoption, inadequate reskilling infrastructure, and insufficient institutional support, whereas organizations implementing proactive reskilling programs achieved 64% higher employee retention. Overall, AI-driven workforce displacement extends beyond job losses, requiring coordinated policy interventions, institutional support, and continuous workforce reskilling to promote equitable labor market transitions, organizational resilience, sustainable employment, and inclusive economic growth in increasingly AI-enabled economies. These findings emphasize collaborative governance, lifelong learning, adaptive leadership, resilient institutions and responsible implementation.
topics: Labor market dynamics and wage inequality

documents.abstract: This study aimed to empirically analyze the relationships of AI risk perception and digital self-efficacy with the use of digital transaction services, digital civic participation, and life satisfaction in the context of a digital society characterized by the proliferation of generative AI. Using data from 7000 members of the general public collected through the “2023 Survey on the Digital Divide,” conducted by the Ministry of Science and ICT and the National Information Society Agency, this study conducted confirmatory factor analysis and structural equation modeling using IBM SPSS Statistics 31.0 and IBM AMOS 31.0. The results showed that AI risk perception was positively associated with the use of digital transaction services and negatively associated with digital civic participation, while its relationship with life satisfaction was not statistically significant. In contrast, digital self-efficacy was positively associated with the use of digital transaction services, digital civic participation, and life satisfaction. These findings demonstrate that digital self-efficacy is a key antecedent in explaining various digital outcomes, whereas AI risk perception has only a limited influence on digital outcomes. By examining AI risk perception and digital self-efficacy within a single integrated model, this study expands the understanding of digital outcomes and suggests that digital policies in the AI era should be pursued not only through risk management but also by strengthening citizens’ digital self-efficacy and digital utilization capabilities.

topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Background/Objectives: The golden hours, the critical initial phase of each criminal investigation, are crucial for securing evidence, engaging witnesses, and directing investigative efforts, yet this phase often relies heavily on individual expertise and intuition. This paper explores how artificial intelligence (AI) can enhance evidence-based and data-driven policing during these early hours by improving decision-making and investigative quality. Methods: Drawing on a source pool of 1589 open-source case records, covering solved and unsolved homicides, suspected homicides, suspicious disappearances, and deaths initially of unclear cause in the Netherlands, compiled from public repositories that aggregate material originating from police files and published court decisions, the study develops a conceptual framework that integrates AI techniques such as automated narrative generation, 3D reconstruction, and digital evidence analysis into early-stage investigations, and illustrates it retrospectively with a purposively selected, coded twenty-case sample; scenario generation in the proposed system follows the twelve elementary scenario components (ESC12). Results: By linking empirical data from previous cases with new operational information, that is, information that emerges or is newly discovered during the ongoing investigation, AI is designed to support the narrative approach, accelerate scenario reconstruction, and generate candidate hypotheses and leads for investigator assessment. An author-assigned preliminary evidence-and-readiness assessment rates four AI application domains against five golden-hour criteria, and the retrospective case analysis maps each framework component onto documented investigative problems. Conclusions: AI may improve investigative efficiency and consistency and is hypothesised to mitigate the impact of cognitive bias and time pressure; these effects remain to be demonstrated in prospective evaluations. Meanwhile, challenges remain regarding explainability, reliability, and ethical compliance.

Purpose This paper examines how regular use of generative AI enhances productivity, but somehow, in contrast, reduces the opportunities for employees to utilize critical thinking skills and translate their hands-on experience into organizational learning. Design/methodology/approach The paper is a problem-based conceptual synthesis linking AI literacy, organizational learning, human-AI collaboration, evidence from knowledge workers, and knowledge collapse theory. On the other hand, human-AI augmentation and disengagement are considered opposing risks from which five workplace safeguards are derived. Findings The paper shows that the issue is not the use of GenAI, but organizations that reward flawless automation output while ignoring verification, human reasoning, and visible employee learning. The paper introduces the THINK framework interlinking organizational practices: Transparency, Human judgment, Intellectual engagement, Navigation of evidence and Knowledge construction. Research limitations/implications The THINK framework conceptual synthesis is selective and not empirically tested. Future research should validate the application effect across different sectors, industries and levels of GenAI adoption. Practical implications The THINK framework can be integrated into employee training, performance management discussions, decision-making and AI governance systems. Originality/value The paper transposes the traditional argument about GenAI-mediated cognition into a simple, auditable framework that managers can apply on the job as coaches, learning professionals, and AI governance teams.

topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education
Technology and Human Factors in Education and Health

documents.abstract: This paper mainly examines whether artificial intelligence (AI) can really improve the efficiency of financial accounting work, and why accountants are still required to verify its outputs and provide necessary supervision. To address these issues, this study reviews academic papers and reports published by professional institutions. Based on these studies, AI has been shown to perform repetitive tasks that follow fixed procedures. In addition, it can process large volumes of transactions, detect potential errors, and use historical data to forecast future sales or cash flows. Thus, AI reduces the time accountants spend on manual processing, thereby enabling them to allocate more time to analyzing financial information and generating valuable business insights. However, if the data provided by the company is incorrect or incomplete, the results may also be inaccurate. Moreover, financial records may contain private information, such as bank details, employee salaries, and customer data. As a result, AI should assist accountants rather than replace them. In this process, accountants still need to verify AI-generated results, review relevant information, make judgments based on the company's actual situation, and take responsibility for final decisions.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: The aim of this study is to examine the transformation caused by artificial intelligence technologies in accounting processes and the effects of this transformation on the employment structure of accounting professionals. With the digital transformation process, artificial intelligence has become widely used in accounting fields such as automation, financial reporting, auditing, risk analysis, and decision support processes. In this study, artificial intelligence technologies, accounting information systems, digital accounting applications, and artificial intelligence-supported accounting processes are discussed, and the effects of technological developments on the accounting profession are evaluated. The findings of the study indicate that artificial intelligence applications increase transaction speed, reduce error rates, and enable more effective use of financial information by automating routine accounting processes. However, artificial intelligence is also changing the roles of accounting professionals; while roles based on data entry are decreasing, new areas of responsibility such as analysis, consulting, and strategic decision support are gaining importance. In this process, digital competencies, data analysis skills, and the ability to use technological tools have become essential requirements for accounting professionals. In conclusion, artificial intelligence is not considered a factor that eliminates the accounting profession but rather a strategic technology that reshapes professional roles. It is expected that hybrid working models, in which human expertise and artificial intelligence work together, will become more widespread in the future.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Cystic acne is a severe inflammatory dermatological condition traditionally associated with genetic, hormonal, and microbial factors. Although environmental exposures may contribute to acne pathogenesis, the role of airborne agricultural irritants remains underexplored. Agricultural environments contain a complex mixture of organic dusts, pesticides, fertilizers, volatile compounds, and animal-derived particulates that may influence skin barrier integrity and inflammatory responses. This narrative review examines the potential relationship between airborne agricultural exposures and cystic acne by integrating evidence from dermatology, environmental health, and immunology. Particular attention is given to mechanisms through which agricultural irritants may disrupt epidermal barrier proteins, including filaggrin and claudins; promote oxidative stress and lipid peroxidation; alter the cutaneous microbiome; and activate inflammatory signaling pathways, including nuclear factor kappa B (NF-κB) and the NLRP3 inflammasome. These processes may contribute to the release of proinflammatory cytokines, including interleukin (IL)-1β, IL-6, tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α), and IL-8, potentially amplifying inflammation within the pilosebaceous unit. The review also explores the possibility that chronic inhalation of agricultural aerosols may contribute to systemic immune activation and influence cutaneous inflammatory responses. While environmental and occupational exposures have been associated with inflammatory skin conditions, direct evidence linking airborne agricultural irritants specifically to cystic acne remains limited. This review highlights potential mechanistic connections, identifies gaps in the current literature, and emphasizes the need for further epidemiological and experimental research to clarify these associations. Understanding the relationship between agricultural airborne exposures and acne may inform future preventive strategies and occupational health considerations.
topics: Acne and Rosacea Treatments and Effects
Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: This study examined academic achievement and multidimensional engagement among Grade 9 Filipino students learning Geometry through a flipped classroom at a Filipino international school in Saudi Arabia. A quasi-experimental one-group pretest–posttest design was used, with total enumerative population sampling and 30 paired achievement observations. Teacher-prepared videos supported pre-class learning during a six-week intervention; classroom sessions emphasized collaborative problem-solving, discussion, and guided exercises. Engagement was assessed through a 20-item Student Engagement Questionnaire covering behavioral, emotional, cognitive, and psychomotor dimensions. Academic achievement was measured with a Geometry Achievement Test. Descriptive statistics, a paired-samples t-test, and Spearman’s rank-order correlation were used. All four engagement dimensions were rated high. Raw achievement increased from M = 15.67 (SD = 2.58) to M = 17.47 (SD = 2.81); transformed scores increased from M = 52.22 (SD = 8.59) to M = 58.22 (SD = 9.38). The achievement difference was statistically significant (t = −2.51, p = .018), with Cohen’s d = −0.46, or 0.46 in magnitude. Cognitive engagement correlated significantly with pre-test achievement (ρ = .397, p = .030), and emotional engagement correlated significantly with post-test achievement (ρ = .390, p = .033). Other correlations were not statistically significant. The findings support contextual consideration of flipped Geometry instruction and informed a proposed teacher professional development program. The one-group design limits causal interpretation and generalization.

This study examines the influence of workplace spirituality and workplace climate on job performance, with intrinsic motivation as a mediating variable, in public sector organizations located in Indonesia’s underdeveloped, frontier, and outermost (3T) regions. A quantitative cross-sectional approach was employed involving 342 employees of the Supiori Regency Government selected through purposive sampling. Data were analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling–Partial Least Squares (SEM-PLS) and Importance Performance Map Analysis (IPMA). The findings indicate that workplace spirituality and workplace climate positively and significantly affect intrinsic motivation and job performance. Workplace spirituality emerged as the strongest predictor of job performance. Intrinsic motivation also significantly mediated the relationship between workplace spirituality, workplace climate, and job performance. The IPMA results reveal that alignment with organizational values, sense of community, and employee involvement in decision-making remain priority areas for organizational improvement. This study highlights the importance of meaningful work and a supportive work environment in sustaining public sector performance within the bureaucratic context of 3T regions while extending the application of Self-Determination Theory in public sector organizations.

Article 50 of the EU AI Act requires generative AI providers to mark synthetic content in a detectable format. This obligation is carried out through a mechanism invisible to end users. The resulting gap leaves accountability around disinformation, copyright infringement, and public trust largely unaddressed. This paper reports a pilot study that probes this transparency–verifiability gap through a comparative document analysis of five major providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Meta, xAI) combined with a small-scale empirical robustness pilot of the open-source SynthID-Text method on GPT-2. The document analysis shows that regulatory disclosure does not equate to an independently verifiable detection mechanism for third parties. In this pilot experiment, watermarked texts scored significantly higher than unwatermarked texts (t(38) = 15.94, p < 0.001, Cohen’s d = 5.04, ROC-AUC = 1.000; Youden’s J-optimal threshold = 0.533, yielding 100% sensitivity and 100% specificity on this intact (uncorrupted) sample; the design was adequately powered (80%) only for effects of d ≥ 0.91 or larger, A calibration/test-separated validation on independent held-out data (n = 320) confirmed this discrimination within the pilot setup (TPR at FPR ≤ 1% = 98.75%), without implying generalization beyond it. This signal, measured with an untrained detector, degraded substantially under a deliberately engineered high-severity stress test (50% word-level corruption), a decline confirmed by Holm-corrected pairwise comparisons across nine of the ten corruption-level pairs (F(4, 56) = 98.39, p < 0.001, generalized η2 = 0.744, r = −0.824). These are preliminary, pilot-scale findings; they indicate that Article 50 guidance should require standardized error-rate reporting and independently auditable detection access, not disclosure alone. They offer an exploratory contribution to the AI ethics literature on transparency and accountability. Given the small open-source backbones (GPT-2, with a replication on Pythia-410M), the primarily untrained detector (a small-scale trained Bayesian detector did not outperform it on intact text), the single watermarking scheme, and the largely synthetic corruption type (only one model-based paraphrase condition was tested), these results remain preliminary, pilot-scale evidence whose generalization to commercial systems, large-scale trained detectors, other watermarking families, and a broader range of realistic paraphrase and translation attacks requires future research.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Introduction Today, sustainable leadership is a strategic leadership approach that addresses environmental, social, and economic priorities from a holistic perspective while at the same time driving digital transformation processes. The research aims to explain how sustainable leaders mobilize organizational resources, technological infrastructure, and human creativity within the framework of Dynamic Capabilities Theory. Methods The research was conducted on 456 white-collar employees working in small and medium-sized enterprises operating in Giresun, Kars, and Kırşehir provinces. The data collected by the convenience sampling method were analyzed using the PLS-SEM method with the SmartPLS 4.1.1 program. Results The analysis results show that sustainable leadership has significant and positive effects on perceptions of artificial intelligence, the generation of creative ideas, digital transformation, and awareness of the circular economy. It was found that the perception of artificial intelligence (AI) has a significant effect on both digital transformation and awareness of the circular economy. It was also determined that creative idea generation has significant effects on digital transformation and awareness of the circular economy. The results of the mediation analyses revealed a partial mediating role for all variables. Discussion The findings reveal that sustainable leadership is not limited to the environmental and social responsibility dimension and is a strategic element that directs digital transformation processes, shapes perceptions towards artificial intelligence, and encourages organizational creativity.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming sports medicine and exercise science, offering unprecedented capabilities in markerless motion capture, automated exercise prescription, diagnostic imaging and integrated athlete monitoring. These advances have the potential to democratise biomechanical analysis, scale clinical expertise to underserved populations and shift injury management from reactive treatment to predictive prevention. However, the pace of adoption carries significant risks, including technological dependency without methodological literacy, the entrenchment of global inequities through biased training datasets and models, the erosion of clinician-athlete relationships and a widening governance vacuum over data ownership and algorithmic accountability. This commentary argues that the next frontier of athletic intelligence will be defined not by technological sophistication alone, but by the wisdom, inclusivity and ethical resolve with which the sports medicine community deploys it. Disciplined engagement (rather than uncritical adoption or reflexive avoidance) is the potential path forward.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: In 2017, Elon Musk stated that humans must augment their mental capabilities through the “merger of biological intelligence and machine intelligence” lest they risk becoming “house cats” to artificial intelligence. In 2024, he successfully implanted his “Neuralink” chip in a human patient. Now, while the idea of improving the human condition by integrating technology into the human body did not begin with Elon Musk, his tangible advancements in neural implants have shifted the ethical questions surrounding them from theoretical to practical. One particularly thorny application of this technology—one that raises both ethical and existential questions—is its use for moral enhancement. Ethically, we must consider whether it is good or bad to employ technology that ensures individuals act morally. Existentially, if human free will is expressed most meaningfully through moral choice, should we be willing to relinquish that freedom for the sake of social harmony, crime prevention, even world peace? Or must we accept a world marked by moral failure, violence, and injustice in order to preserve human autonomy? To address these questions, I examine contemporary philosophical debates surrounding moral enhancement and place them in dialogue with classical Jewish sources. For, as will be shown, Jewish thought offers a unique framework for addressing both the ethical permissibility of moral enhancement and the existential tension between free will and moral perfection. By juxtaposing cutting-edge neurotechnology with ancient moral anthropology, this paper invites a reassessment of what it means to be human in an age increasingly capable of reshaping human agency itself.

This article examines the transformative impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on English language learning (ELL). It explores how AI-driven technologies—such as natural language processing (NLP), intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning algorithms, and speech recognition—facilitate personalized instruction, enhance autonomous learning, and provide immediate diagnostic feedback. Furthermore, the paper discusses the pedagogical advantages, potential limitations, and future implications of integrating AI into modern language classrooms.

Abstract Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) has shifted from voluntary philanthropy to a core governance domain in which stakeholders demand verifiable evidence of social and environmental performance. Yet CSR reporting remains plagued by greenwashing, inconsistent metrics, and assurance practices that are largely point-in-time and self-interested. This paper examines how artificial intelligence (AI) can strengthen transparency and accountability in CSR initiatives. Drawing on a structured review of peer-reviewed literature and authoritative institutional reports published between 2011 and 2024, the paper develops a conceptual framework that maps four AI capabilities—natural language processing, machine-learning anomaly detection, blockchain-enabled distributed ledgers, and conversational AI—to four CSR mechanisms: dis-closure verification, real-time monitoring, traceability-based assurance, and participatory stake-holder engagement. The analysis argues that these mechanisms collectively reduce information asymmetry, harmonise divergent ESG ratings, and operationalise the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) and the Artificial Intelligence Act. The paper also identifies critical limitations, including the “black-box accountability paradox”, algorithmic bias, data-quality constraints, and a widening digital divide between multinational enterprises and small and medium-sized firms. It concludes that AI is a necessary but insufficient enabler: realising its transformative potential requires combined progress on data standards, third-party model audits, regulatory sandboxes, and meaningful stakeholder participation in AI governance. Keywords: corporate social responsibility; artificial intelligence; transparency; accountability; ESG; greenwashing; blockchain; corporate governance.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Suicide is a leading cause of death, accounting for one million deaths annually worldwide (World Health Organisation, 2014). A large number of people attempt suicide, with some researchers estimating that there are approximately 25 attempts for every death (Goldsmith et al., 2002). According to the World Health Organisation, someone dies by suicide somewhere in the world every 40 seconds. Guyana is a rural country in the north-eastern corner of South America, with a population of around 740,000. It has recorded the highest suicide rates in the world for several reasons, the most significant of which are poverty, alcoholism and easy access to lethal pesticides. To better understand how risk factors interact, Franklin and his colleagues applied machine learning to the electronic health records of over 5,000 people with a history of self-harm. They developed an algorithm that predicted suicide attempts based on a range of risk factors, including demographic data, previous diagnoses, medication history and previous healthcare usage (Walsh et al., 2017). Franklin says: “Machine learning can take us from near-random guesswork to predictions that are about 80% accurate.” Therefore, through this intervention, we aim to determine the extent to which artificial intelligence can predict suicidal thoughts and, consequently, to attempt to identify mechanisms for preventing them and reducing the rate of suicide attempts.

The world is witnessing a rapid digital transformation that imposes itself as a fundamental pillar for developing the efficiency of the educational system. In the Syrian context, this transformation acquires highly critical strategic dimensions; it is not merely an immaterial process or a modern luxury. Rather, from one perspective, it represents an essential tool to overcome the repercussions of crises and dismantle material relationships of digital dependency. From another perspective, it serves as a qualified vehicle for building human capital, paving the way for the sustainable reconstruction phase in line with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) 2015. The research problem lies in the gap between the requirements of digital transformation and the actual reality of the higher education sector in Syria, which faces severe infrastructural, technical, and funding challenges. Consequently, this study seeks to answer the primary question: How can digital transformation in the higher education system contribute effectively and independently-far from digital dependency-to enhancing human capital skills to meet the requirements of sustainable development and the post-war reconstruction phase in Syria? This study aims to diagnose the reality of digitization within the higher education sector in Syria (opportunities and challenges), foresee the role of digital transformation and artificial intelligence in equipping graduates with required sustainable future skills, and provide a matrix of actionable recommendations, practical solutions, and flexible, low-cost alternatives applicable within available local capabilities. The study adopts a descriptive-analytical approach by reviewing local and international literature and official institutional reports relevant to the higher education system and the requirements of digital transformation and the labour market

Teaching in special and inclusive education presents unique emotional and ecological demands, yet the specific psychological mechanisms through which social–emotional learning (SEL) competencies relate to how teachers navigate these challenges remain underexplored. Therefore, the present study investigates the pathways linking educators’ SEL and intrinsic motivation to their psychological well-being. In this cross-sectional study, 459 educators completed self-report questionnaires assessing their SEL competencies, intrinsic motivation, teacher self-efficacy, perceived work stress, and psychological well-being. The findings show that both SEL competencies and intrinsic motivation are positively associated with teacher self-efficacy, which in turn is negatively related to perceived work stress and positively associated with psychological well-being. Furthermore, a multigroup path analysis comparing educators in special-education settings with those in inclusive environments revealed no statistically significant differences in these pathways between the two contexts. However, the substantial disparity in group sizes warrants cautious interpretation of this finding. By illuminating the interplay between internal socio-emotional resources and occupational stress, this research highlights the potential protective value of SEL competencies in relation to educator well-being across diverse and demanding educational contexts.

Large language models have developed from fluent next-token generators into integrated systems capable of reasoning, coding, multimodal interpretation, retrieval, tool use and increasingly persistent agentic action. This monograph reviews ten influential global systems: OpenAI GPT-5-class ChatGPT, Anthropic Claude, Google Gemini, xAI Grok, DeepSeek, Moonshot Kimi, Alibaba Qwen, Mistral, Perplexity and Obsidian. They are not all equivalent objects. GPT, Claude, Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek, Kimi, Qwen and Mistral are model families; Perplexity is primarily a retrieval-and-research architecture that orchestrates models and sources; Obsidian is a human-owned knowledge environment in which language models may be embedded. The review therefore avoids a misleading single benchmark league table and instead compares eight dimensions: reasoning, factual reliability, coding and agency, multimodality, context and retrieval, openness and deployment, governance and safety, and support for durable human meaning-making. Published system cards and developer documentation show large gains in benchmark performance and reductions in factual error, but none establishes that probabilistic model competence is equivalent to human understanding, selfhood or conscious learning. The strongest common limitation is not simply hallucination. It is the absence of an explicit, inspectable architecture for the transition from observation to question, from question to perspective, from perspective to interpretation, from interpretation to choice, and from choice to reconstructed meaning. This is where cCC* is positioned as a research proposition rather than as another foundation model: Curiosity → Chances → Choices → Changes, interpreted through AEIOUF perspectives, SELF ↔ OTHER distinction, P M ΘΦ guardrails, and the recursive NEWCON → INCON → RECON → NEXT? cycle. The monograph concludes that current systems are increasingly powerful at producing and acting upon representations, while Natural Learning asks a different question: how does an embodied human observer construct, contest, share and recursively reconstruct meaning?

Synthetic data can support machine-learning research when real observations are scarce, sensitive, expensive, or difficult to share, but synthetic status and dataset size do not establish utility, representativeness, privacy, or fairness. This focused narrative review synthesizes selected research on generation methods, predictive utility, fidelity and diversity, subgroup representation, privacy, fairness-aware generation, recursive training, and large-language-model-generated data. The evidence indicates that suitability is conditional: generated data must preserve information relevant to the intended task, represent important and rare patterns, and be assessed for subgroup disparities and disclosure risks. Results from recursive-training studies further show that repeated reliance on generated data can reduce distributional coverage under some conditions, although the risk depends on the training setup and the availability of real data. Because the reviewed studies use different domains, datasets, methods, and metrics, they do not support a universal ranking of synthetic-data methods. The paper’s central contribution is a proposed integrated evaluation framework that brings together six dimensions—predictive utility, fidelity, diversity, subgroup fairness, privacy, and recursive-data risk—and explains why they should be considered together rather than treated as interchangeable measures. The review is narrative rather than systematic: sources were selected for relevance and influence, no exhaustive screening process was performed, and the synthesis is not a complete census of the field. The framework is conceptual and has not been empirically validated in this paper. The findings support use-case-specific evaluation, transparent reporting, subgroup analysis, documented data lineage, and direct assessment of privacy claims.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Objectives Stigma is an important structural determinant of occupational health and safety in sex work, whereby gaps remain in understanding the complexity of the phenomenon. This article examines anticipated, experienced, internalized, layered, perceived, and secondary stigmas, and explores how they affect occupational risks pertaining to sex workers’ access to services, private lives, health, violence, and careers. It also explores how stigmas are manifested in different legislative models regulating sex work.Methods A PRISMA-guided systematic review of peer-reviewed empirical studies published between 2010 and 2020 was conducted using a centralized academic search system enabling simultaneous searches across major databases and publisher platforms, such as Web of Science, Scopus, JSTOR, SAGE, EMERALD, PubMed, MEDLINE, ScienceDirect, and EBSCO. A total of 90 qualitative, quantitative, and mixed methods studies published globally met the eligibility criteria and were analyzed through systematic data extraction and coding.Results The results demonstrate that stigma functions as a complex system of discrimination in which different types of stigma operate simultaneously across occupational domains. The evidence most consistently highlights the negative effects of experienced, anticipated, and internalized stigmas, particularly regarding access to services and impacts on private life. Occupational risks where different stigmas most intensely intersect include increased vulnerability for STIs, mental distress, and barriers to the utilization of services. The reviewed studies further suggest that stigma-related occupational risks may manifest differently across legislative models, with more adverse effects reported in criminalizing and otherwise repressive legal contexts.Conclusions Different types of stigma intersect and build an interconnected web transcending occupational risks and legislative models concerning sex work. Our findings emphasize the need to address stigma as critical occupational risk that requires sustained research and targeted policy interventions, conceptualizing it as a complex, structural, and intersectional phenomenon.

Extended reasoning has substantially improved multimodal large language models (MLLMs) on tasks requiring compositional and relational inference. However, multimodal grounding imposes a distinct requirement: reasoning must ultimately converge on a target-specific compact representation that supports precise localization. As reasoning trajectories grow longer, they often expand into broad scene narratives and peripheral relational details, which can dilute grounded perceptual evidence and lead to ambiguous or incorrect predictions. Motivated by the information bottleneck principle, we propose Think-Compress-Answer (TCA), a reinforcement learning framework that decomposes multimodal grounding into three phases: free-form reasoning, target-aware context compression, and answer generation conditioned on the compressed context. TCA is optimized through a multi-stage Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) with progressive rewards that establish the structured output protocol, minimize reasoning-specific information while preserving target-relevant content, and directly improve localization accuracy. This staged design enables MLLMs to retain the benefits of extended reasoning while distilling it into the minimal context required for grounding. Experiments across six multimodal grounding benchmarks show that TCA attains substantial zero-shot performance gains, demonstrating the effectiveness of reasoning compression.

Large language models (LLMs) have recently shown strong potential for time series reasoning, while models that reason over time series are usually with long chains of thought. However, this process often consumes thousands of tokens, directly leading to substantial latency during inference. In contrast, System 1 models such as Jev make decisions instantly and can naturally be an alternative, but raw time series are not compatible with the embedding space of these models, thus hindering the reasoning performance, especially when input series contain thousands of numeric points. In this paper, we make a very early attempt to propose a time series System 1 model, namely TimesJev. Specifically, we first formalize System 1 sufficiency in time series reasoning, which motivates a compressed representation for time series with key frequency patterns preserved. To construct this representation, we derive a dimension reduction objective that combines (i) a sufficiency divergence that measures the core information lost during compression, and (ii) a realizability divergence that quantifies the incompatibility of the System 1 model to the optimal prediction given this representation. We optimize this objective by learning time series compression with a gating mechanism for sufficiency, and then aligning the selected representation with the embedding space for realizability. Finally, experiments on 13 datasets demonstrate that TimesJev outperforms reasoning models by over 62% with 62.9% less inference time than their fine-tuned versions on average.

Expert human readers process large inputs (e.g., code repositories and long documents) by skimming to closely read only what matters. On the other hand, language models process all input tokens through each model layer, resulting in significant processing costs for long-context inputs. We introduce TokenGate, a small, drop-in component that extends existing trained models to enable end-to-end learnable token pruning over long-context inputs for fast and memory-efficient prefill. To enable end-to-end learning despite the non-differentiable top-K operator for token pruning, we introduce token-gated attention, a mechanism inspired by Mixture-of-Experts that re-weights attention logits using token importance scores. Across diverse tasks, TokenGate achieves $1.4$-$11.3\times$ faster time-to-first token (TTFT) and $1.5$-$3.4\times$ lower peak memory at no accuracy degradation for prefill in transformers. Compared to the best-performing prior methods for token-pruning, TokenGate gives up to $6.4\times$ faster prefill and $2\times$ lower peak memory. TokenGate natively extends both standard transformers (e.g., Qwen3) and hybrid-attention models (e.g., Qwen3.5) with simple lightweight adaptation comparable to standard parameter-efficient fine-tuning. We make our code available at: https://github.com/tokengate-models/TokenGate.

Artificial intelligence (AI) and learning analytics are transforming higher education by enabling personalised learning, adaptive support, and data-informed decision-making. These developments present significant opportunities for improving educational inclusion for students with learning difficulties, yet they also introduce challenges relating to privacy, algorithmic bias, explainability, accessibility, and governance. Although Kuwait has strengthened disability legislation while simultaneously investing in AI-enabled education under Kuwait Vision 2035, these policy agendas have largely evolved independently. Similar governance gaps are evident across the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), where disability inclusion, AI adoption, and higher education reform remain weakly integrated. This conceptual paper develops the AI- and Learning-Analytics-Enabled Inclusive Support Framework for Learning Difficulties (ISF-LD) to guide the responsible implementation of AI within inclusive higher education. Using a conceptual framework development methodology, the study synthesises evidence from four complementary domains: research on learning difficulties and disability inclusion; scholarship on AI, learning analytics, and responsible AI; national and international policy documents; and established educational and disability theories. The framework is informed by six theoretical perspectives: the Social Model of Disability, Universal Design for Learning, Sociocultural Theory, Self-Determination Theory, learning analytics ethics, and responsible AI principles. The proposed framework comprises five interconnected implementation layers: national policy and governance, institutional leadership and disability services, faculty capability, AI-enabled inclusive pedagogy and assessment, and student self-determination. These layers operate through an iterative, non-linear governance model in which each layer informs and is informed by the others, supported by four cross-cutting principles: rights-based governance, stigma-aware disclosure, universal accessibility, and responsible AI. Together, they position AI as a governed educational capability that supports inclusion while safeguarding learner autonomy, transparency, and institutional accountability. The paper contributes to the literature in three ways. First, it integrates disability studies, AI governance, learning analytics, and inclusive higher education within a single conceptual model. Second, it addresses an important policy gap by linking disability inclusion with AI governance in the context of Kuwait and the GCC. Third, it proposes a theoretically grounded and empirically testable framework that can inform institutional strategy, educational policy, and future research on responsible AI in higher education. Although developed within Kuwait, the ISF-LD offers a transferable governance model for universities seeking to implement AI ethically while advancing equitable and inclusive learning.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Teacher preparation depends on deliberate practice with learners who have identifiable strengths and weaknesses, yet classroom experience accumulates slowly and is hard to standardize. Language-model-simulated students could offer scalable, repeatable practice, but only if a simulated learner can exhibit a specified answer-performance profile rather than behaving as a uniformly capable assistant. We introduce a benchmark for controllable learner simulation in school mathematics: the target condition is a binary vector of retained and suppressed curricular skill families, and we measure how faithfully a language model’s answer behavior realizes that profile via profile-alignment, retained-versus-forgotten, and cross-skill analyses. Across three models and two grades, selective suppression can be induced and measured, yet higher mathematical capability did not imply stronger controllability among the evaluated models: a model can solve the mathematics well yet be the weakest at selective suppression (bootstrap selectivity index 0.35 to 0.70). Induced errors are systematic: independent models converge on the same wrong answers, and an exploratory single-coder analysis found many compaible with documented error categories. Evidence is answer-level (single turn, multiple choice) at Grades 4 and 5. These results show that answer-level skill-profile controllability can be measured as one prerequisite for studying LLM-based learner simulation in teacher-preparation and assessment research.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Large language models acquire broad knowledge from web-scale corpora during pretraining, including knowledge that could be hazardous if misused. Removing such knowledge from the model itself without degrading general capability is desirable but difficult, as it is deeply entangled with general capability within the same parameters. Existing safety alignment and unlearning methods typically adjust these shared parameters, tending to suppress the expression of hazardous knowledge rather than remove it. As a result, the knowledge remains in the model and is readily recoverable by subsequent fine-tuning. To address this limitation, we propose REX (Relocating into Removable EXperts), a knowledge relocation method that separates hazardous knowledge from general capability at the architectural level. Exploiting the modular structure of Mixture-of-Experts models, REX expands the model with a set of new, physically removable experts designated to hold hazardous knowledge. Through expert expansion, selective gradient masking and routing differentiation, it relocates hazardous knowledge out of the original experts and concentrates it in the new ones. Excising these new experts yields a model suitable for public release. This removal holds consistently across Intern-S2, Qwen3.5-35B-A3B and Gemma-4-26B-A4B; on Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, for instance, excision lowers WMDP-Bio accuracy by 48.4 points while MMLU changes by less than 3 points. The excised model matches the strongest of nine unlearning baselines in removing hazardous knowledge, and it is the only one that preserves this removal under subsequent fine-tuning. After 250M tokens of standard fine-tuning on Qwen3.5, the best baseline rebounds on WMDP-Bio from 44.1% to 78.3%, whereas REX rises only from 32.4% to 42.8%.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This study examines the adoption, use, and institutionalisation of big data and artificial intelligence in official statistics in Latin America and the Caribbean, drawing on the 2024 and 2025 International Consultations conducted with National Statistical Offices. The study combines questionnaire data from 15 responding countries in 2024 and 21 countries and territories in 2025 with qualitative evidence from in-depth interviews. It also proposes the Statistical Innovation Index, a composite indicator designed to approximate differences in the adoption, integration, and institutionalisation of big data and AI across NSOs. Results indicate a gradual consolidation of big data use, although applications remain concentrated in web scraping and satellite imagery, particularly for price, population, environmental, and agricultural statistics. AI adoption remains at an earlier stage: 39% of responding NSOs reported its use, mainly in data processing and other operational tasks. The maturity classification reveals substantial heterogeneity across the region, with most NSOs concentrated in early or emerging stages of statistical innovation. Findings suggest that progress follows a selective process in which exploratory initiatives are gradually filtered into a smaller number of sustainable applications. Institutional capacity, governance, infrastructure, and regional cooperation emerge as key enablers of this process. More broadly, the findings suggest that the transition from exploratory to operational uses of big data and AI reflects an evolving institutional role of NSOs, in which technological innovation is accompanied by new responsibilities for data governance, institutional coordination, and maintaining public trust in official statistics.

Universities increasingly orchestrate teaching and learning through compound configurations that span spaces, devices, timetables and roles. As digital content and workflows increasingly shape physical estates, and vice versa, alignment frames overlook the compound, cross-host configurations already in motion. In this article we ask whether estate-level orchestration, rather than digital–physical alignment alone, should be the operative unit of design for planning and delivering student experiences across and beyond campus. We draw on three exemplars at a research-intensive university: (1) a theatre-scale interactive three-dimensional system, which streams or web-delivers interactive three-dimension into traditional lecture theatres and learners’ devices; (2) a high-fidelity virtual reality digital twin of a chemistry lab for pre-lab rehearsal; and (3) space-planning web apps for co-design and decision support. From these, we sketch a purpose-orientated, configuration-first stance and situate it within work on cyber-/smart-campus estates, learning ecologies, TPACK and postdigital perspectives. Beyond education, digital-first space planning is already operational at scale, including in automotive manufacturing (BMW Group), cultural architecture (Dubai Museum of the Future) and national infrastructure (National Grid’s Triton platform). Higher education has both the conceptual case and, in several respects, the enabling conditions to follow. Hence, we argue that the convergence of immersive, computational and spatial technologies is expanding what institutions can compose and deliver, making device-label categories less useful for both learning and space design. This configuration-first stance is also directly applicable to the governance of artificial intelligence in higher education: as with earlier technology labels, institutions risk misallocating attention and resource if ‘artificial intelligence’ is treated as a discrete category rather than as a family of capabilities, from generative code or audiovisual models to computer vision and wearable ‘artificial intelligence’, some of which already permeate the configurations described here. We conclude with operational implications and a call for institutions to transcend their siloed functions and budgets, by elevating orchestration (not devices, spaces or platforms) as the primary unit of design.

Action-conditioned video generative models trained on successful, goal-directed demonstrations tend to ignore the commanded action, rendering a plausible expert-like future regardless of what is asked of them. We trace this failure to training data that lack sufficient action influence. We analyze this metric and prove that it upper bounds the action influence that any model trained on that data can express. Expert demonstrations, whose narrow action distributions let next states be predicted without attending to the action, set a low ceiling that no amount of model capacity alone can raise. Raising it requires collecting different data. We introduce Action Influence Maximization (AIM), an algorithm for actively collecting training data for improving dataset action influence. We compare the performance and data-efficiency of AIM against exploration heuristics and intrinsic-motivation methods on simulated navigation and manipulation tasks. In pixel-based manipulation, AIM is the only method that consistently improves controllability: 500 actively collected episodes added to 3k demonstrations match a world model trained on 300k expert episodes on end-effector controllability, an $85\times$ reduction in data.

Training a machine learning (ML) model is an optimization process that typically requires a set of examples with ground-truth labels beforehand. Obtaining these ground truths usually requires laborious human effort and can be costly. The scalability of human labeling becomes a concern when there are a large number of data points that need to be labeled. To address this practical issue, we consider an optimization setting where a subset of samples has ground-truth labels, while the remaining data points were labeled by an ML predictor, which could potentially assign incorrect labels to those points. We propose both first-order and zeroth-order stochastic optimization methods for training on datasets consisting of a mix of true-labeled and ML-labeled samples. We further conduct comprehensive empirical studies from training a linear regression model to fine-tuning a large language model (LLM) to showcase the effectiveness of the proposed algorithms for training with ML-labeled data.
